title: Query Data (SELECT)
structure:
SELECT
  column1,
  column2
FROM table_name
[WHERE condition]
[ORDER BY column_name];
example:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  first_name,
  last_name
FROM customer
ORDER BY customer_id
LIMIT 10;
output:
customer_id | first_name | last_name
-------------+------------+-----------
           1 | MARY       | SMITH
           2 | PATRICIA   | JOHNSON
           3 | LINDA      | WILLIAMS
...
note: Name columns explicitly. SELECT * silently changes result shape when schemas change and can fetch expensive or sensitive fields.

title: DDL Commands
output:
CREATE TABLE
ALTER TABLE
DROP TABLE
note: DDL can take locks and block applications. Review lock behavior and make destructive migrations reversible.

title: DML Commands
example:
CREATE TEMP TABLE customer_note AS
SELECT
  customer_id,
  'Preferred contact: email'::text AS note_text
FROM customer
WHERE customer_id = 1;

INSERT INTO customer_note (
  customer_id,
  note_text
)
SELECT
  customer_id,
  'Preferred contact: phone'
FROM customer
WHERE customer_id = 2;

UPDATE customer_note
SET note_text = 'Preferred contact: SMS'
WHERE customer_id = 1;

DELETE FROM customer_note
WHERE customer_id = 2;
note: Run the same WHERE clause as SELECT first and check its count. Use a transaction for multi-step changes.

title: Filtering Data
structure:
SELECT column_list
FROM table_name
WHERE condition1
  [AND | OR condition2]
ORDER BY column_name;
example:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  first_name,
  last_name,
  active
FROM customer
WHERE active = 1
  AND first_name ILIKE 'A%'
  AND customer_id BETWEEN 1 AND 100
ORDER BY last_name;
output:
customer_id | first_name | last_name | active
-------------+------------+-----------+--------
          53 | ANDREA     | HENDERSON |      1
          80 | ANGELA     | HERNANDEZ |      1
...
note: A leading wildcard, such as ILIKE '%term', usually defeats a normal B-tree index. Measure and use a suitable search index when needed.

title: SQL Joins (Basics)
structure:
SELECT
  left_table.column1,
  right_table.column2
FROM left_table
[INNER | LEFT | RIGHT] JOIN right_table
  ON right_table.key = left_table.key;
example:
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.first_name,
  a.address
FROM customer AS c
INNER JOIN address AS a
  ON a.address_id = c.address_id;

SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  r.rental_id
FROM customer AS c
LEFT JOIN rental AS r
  ON r.customer_id = c.customer_id;
note: Keep relationship predicates in ON. A right-table filter in WHERE can inadvertently turn a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.

title: SQL Joins (Advanced)
structure:
SELECT columns
FROM table_a
JOIN bridge_table
  ON ...
JOIN table_b
  ON ...;

SELECT columns
FROM table_a
CROSS JOIN table_b;

SELECT columns
FROM table_a
WHERE EXISTS (
  subquery
);
example:
SELECT
  f.title,
  cat.name AS category
FROM film AS f
JOIN film_category AS fc
  ON fc.film_id = f.film_id
JOIN category AS cat
  ON cat.category_id = fc.category_id;

SELECT c.customer_id
FROM customer AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM rental AS r
  WHERE r.customer_id = c.customer_id
);
output:
title       | category
------------------+----------
 ACADEMY DINOSAUR | Documentary
 ACE GOLDFINGER   | Horror
...

 customer_id
-------------
           1
...
note: Many-to-many joins multiply rows. Establish the intended grain before aggregating; DISTINCT can hide, not repair, a bad join.

title: Set Operators
structure:
SELECT column_list
FROM query_a
UNION [ALL] | INTERSECT | EXCEPT
SELECT column_list
FROM query_b;
example:
SELECT first_name
FROM customer
UNION
SELECT first_name
FROM staff;

SELECT customer_id
FROM customer
INTERSECT
SELECT customer_id
FROM rental;

SELECT customer_id
FROM customer
EXCEPT
SELECT customer_id
FROM rental;
note: UNION removes duplicates and may need a costly de-duplication step. Use UNION ALL unless set semantics are required.

title: SQL Functions
structure:
SELECT function_name(column1) AS derived_value
FROM table_name;
example:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  upper(first_name) AS first_name_upper,
  length(last_name) AS last_name_length,
  coalesce(email, 'unknown') AS email
FROM customer
LIMIT 10;
note: A function applied to a filtered column can prevent an ordinary index from being used. Verify the plan before optimizing.

title: String Functions
structure:
SELECT
  CONCAT(column1, ' ', column2) AS combined_text,
  UPPER(column1) AS upper_text
FROM table_name;
example:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  concat(first_name, ' ', last_name) AS full_name,
  upper(last_name) AS last_name_upper,
  left(email, 5) AS email_prefix,
  replace(email, '.org', '.example') AS masked_domain
FROM customer
LIMIT 10;
output:
customer_id | full_name        | last_name_upper | email_prefix
-------------+------------------+-----------------+-------------
           1 | MARY SMITH       | SMITH           | MARY.
           2 | PATRICIA JOHNSON | JOHNSON         | PATRI
...
note: CONCAT and the concatenation operator can handle NULL differently. Decide whether a missing value should be empty or remain unknown.

title: Numeric Functions
structure:
SELECT
  numeric_column,
  ROUND(expression, decimal_places) AS rounded_value
FROM table_name;
example:
SELECT
  payment_id,
  amount,
  round(amount * 1.10, 2) AS amount_with_tax,
  abs(amount - 5.00) AS distance_from_five,
  ceil(amount) AS rounded_up
FROM payment
LIMIT 10;
note: Use fixed-precision decimal types for money, not floating point. Define rounding at the business boundary.

title: Date and Time Functions
structure:
SELECT
  timestamp_column,
  CAST(timestamp_column AS DATE) AS date_value,
  date_function(timestamp_column) AS derived_value
FROM table_name
WHERE timestamp_column >= date_value;
example:
SELECT
  rental_id,
  rental_date,
  return_date,
  rental_date::date AS rental_day,
  date_trunc('month', rental_date) AS rental_month,
  return_date - rental_date AS rental_duration
FROM rental
WHERE rental_date >= date '2005-06-01'
LIMIT 10;
note: Use half-open timestamp ranges (>= start AND < next_start) to preserve index use and avoid end-of-day precision bugs.

title: NULL Functions
structure:
SELECT
  COALESCE(column_name, fallback_value) AS value,
  NULLIF(value1, value2) AS nullable_value
FROM table_name;
example:
SELECT
  rental_id,
  coalesce(return_date, now()) AS effective_return_date,
  nullif(staff_id, 0) AS nullable_staff_id
FROM rental
LIMIT 10;
note: COALESCE can mask data-quality issues. Preserve raw NULLs in analytical layers unless a business default is defined.

title: Case Statement
structure:
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN condition1 THEN result1
    WHEN condition2 THEN result2
    ELSE fallback_result
  END AS label
FROM table_name;
example:
SELECT
  payment_id,
  amount,
  CASE
    WHEN amount >= 8 THEN 'high'
    WHEN amount >= 4 THEN 'medium'
    ELSE 'low'
  END AS payment_band
FROM payment
LIMIT 10;
note: CASE stops at the first match. Order overlapping conditions from most specific to least specific and test boundaries.

title: Aggregate Functions
structure:
SELECT
  group_column,
  COUNT(*) AS row_count,
  SUM(numeric_column) AS total_value
FROM table_name
[WHERE row_condition]
GROUP BY group_column
[HAVING aggregate_condition];
example:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  count(*) AS payment_count,
  sum(amount) AS total_paid,
  avg(amount) AS average_payment
FROM payment
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING sum(amount) >= 100
ORDER BY total_paid DESC;
note: WHERE filters source rows; HAVING filters aggregated groups. Do not use HAVING for row-level conditions.

title: Window Functions Basics
structure:
SELECT
  columns,
  aggregate_function(value) OVER (PARTITION BY group_column) AS window_value
FROM table_name;
example:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  payment_id,
  amount,
  avg(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_avg_payment
FROM payment
ORDER BY customer_id, payment_id;
note: Window functions keep the original row count. Large partitions can require costly sorting and memory.

title: Window Aggregate
structure:
SELECT
  columns,
  SUM(value) OVER (PARTITION BY group_column ORDER BY sort_column ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM table_name;
example:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  payment_date,
  amount,
  sum(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date, payment_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM payment
ORDER BY customer_id, payment_date, payment_id;
note: Specify ROWS explicitly. The default frame can treat equal ORDER BY values as peers rather than incremental rows.

title: Window Ranking
structure:
SELECT
  columns,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group_column ORDER BY sort_column DESC) AS row_number
FROM table_name;
example:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  payment_id,
  amount,
  row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC) AS row_num,
  rank() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC) AS payment_rank,
  dense_rank() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY amount DESC) AS dense_payment_rank
FROM payment;
note: Add a stable tie-breaker when order matters. Without one, ROW_NUMBER can vary between executions.

title: Window Value
structure:
SELECT
  columns,
  LAG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY group_column ORDER BY sort_column) AS previous_value,
  LEAD(value) OVER (PARTITION BY group_column ORDER BY sort_column) AS next_value
FROM table_name;
example:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  payment_date,
  amount,
  lag(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date, payment_id) AS previous_amount,
  lead(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date, payment_id) AS next_amount,
  first_value(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY payment_date, payment_id) AS first_amount
FROM payment;
note: FIRST_VALUE observes the current frame. Set an explicit frame when you need a value across the full partition.

title: Subqueries
structure:
SELECT column_list
FROM outer_table
WHERE column_name IN (
  SELECT column_name
  FROM inner_table
  WHERE condition
);
example:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  first_name,
  last_name
FROM customer
WHERE customer_id IN (
  SELECT customer_id
  FROM payment
  GROUP BY customer_id
  HAVING sum(amount) >= 100
);
output:
customer_id | first_name | last_name
-------------+------------+----------
         148 | ELEANOR    | HUNT
         178 | MARION     | SNYDER
...
note: For existence checks, EXISTS avoids NULL-related surprises from NOT IN. Compare plans rather than assuming one form always wins.

title: Common Table Expressions (CTE)
structure:
WITH result_name AS (
  SELECT columns
  FROM table_name
  WHERE condition
)
SELECT columns
FROM result_name;
example:
WITH customer_spend AS (
  SELECT
    customer_id,
    sum(amount) AS total_paid
  FROM payment
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.first_name,
  cs.total_paid
FROM customer AS c
JOIN customer_spend AS cs
  ON cs.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY cs.total_paid DESC;
note: CTEs improve readability but are not automatically faster. Engines differ on whether they materialize or inline them.

title: Views
example:
CREATE VIEW customer_payment_summary AS
SELECT
  customer_id,
  count(*) AS payment_count,
  sum(amount) AS total_paid
FROM payment
GROUP BY customer_id;

SELECT *
FROM customer_payment_summary
ORDER BY total_paid DESC;

DROP VIEW customer_payment_summary;
output:
CREATE VIEW
 customer_id | payment_count | total_paid
-------------+---------------+-----------
         148 |            45 |    211.55
...
DROP VIEW
note: A standard view stores its query, not its result. Treat it as an API and keep its columns and semantics stable.

title: CTAS and Temp Tables
example:
CREATE TEMP TABLE recent_rentals AS
SELECT
  rental_id,
  customer_id,
  rental_date
FROM rental
WHERE rental_date >= date '2005-07-01';

SELECT count(*)
FROM recent_rentals;
note: Temporary tables are session-scoped but still consume resources. Index large temporary datasets used in repeated joins.

title: Stored Procedures
note: Document procedure side effects and transaction behavior; this differs by database and calling context.

title: Triggers
structure:
CREATE TRIGGER trigger_name
BEFORE | AFTER INSERT | UPDATE | DELETE ON table_name
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE trigger_function;
output:
CREATE FUNCTION
CREATE TRIGGER
DROP TRIGGER
DROP FUNCTION
note: Triggers make writes implicit and may amplify bulk work. Keep them minimal and document their side effects.

title: Indexes
output:
CREATE INDEX
 payment_id | amount
------------+-------
      16017 |  5.99
      16018 |  0.99
...
DROP INDEX
note: Every index costs storage and writes. Design composite indexes from real predicates and verify actual use with the planner.

title: Execution Plan
structure:
EXPLAIN [ANALYZE] [options]
SELECT columns
FROM table_name
WHERE condition;
example:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  sum(p.amount) AS total_paid
FROM customer AS c
JOIN payment AS p
  ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE p.payment_date >= timestamp '2005-06-01'
GROUP BY c.customer_id;
output:
HashAggregate  (cost=... rows=... width=...) (actual time=... rows=599 loops=1)
   Group Key: c.customer_id
   ->  Hash Join  (cost=... rows=... width=...)
         Hash Cond: (p.customer_id = c.customer_id)
...
note: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement. Do not point it at an unbounded mutation in production.

title: Partitions
example:
CREATE TABLE payment_archive (
  payment_id integer NOT NULL,
  customer_id smallint NOT NULL,
  payment_date timestamp NOT NULL,
  amount numeric(5,2) NOT NULL
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (payment_date);

CREATE TABLE payment_archive_2005_06
PARTITION OF payment_archive
FOR VALUES FROM ('2005-06-01') TO ('2005-07-01');

INSERT INTO payment_archive (
  payment_id,
  customer_id,
  payment_date,
  amount
)
SELECT
  payment_id,
  customer_id,
  payment_date,
  amount
FROM payment
WHERE payment_date >= timestamp '2005-06-01'
  AND payment_date < timestamp '2005-07-01';
note: Partitioning needs a retention, indexing, and partition-creation strategy. Pruning only works when predicates align with the partition key.
